questions.question: Why does the `messages` field in a LangGraph State TypedDict need `Annotated[list, add_messages]`?
options: It enables streaming of token deltas from the model as they're generated, rather than merging or appending anything.
It compresses the message list when checkpoints are written to disk, trimming older turns to save storage space.
Without the reducer, node updates overwrite the list instead of appending, so every turn loses the prior history.
It converts plain dicts into LangChain message objects at runtime, independent of how list updates get merged.
questions.explanation: Every state field has a reducer; the default is overwrite. `add_messages` makes the message list accumulate instead. Forgetting it is the most common LangGraph bug -- the second node to update `messages` silently wins and prior turns vanish.

questions.question: What is the difference between `interrupt_before=['tools']` and `interrupt_after=['tools']`?
options: No difference; they are aliases for the same hook, and both pause execution at exactly the same point in the graph's node boundary., with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
`interrupt_before` is meant for unit tests where you mock tool calls; `interrupt_after` is meant only for production traffic.
`interrupt_before` pauses after the model emits tool_calls but before the tools execute; `interrupt_after` pauses after the tools have already run.
`interrupt_before` runs the tool in an isolated sandbox first; `interrupt_after` always runs the same tool in production.
questions.explanation: Interrupts stop execution at a node boundary. `interrupt_before` catches the proposed tool call before any side effect happens, which is why approvals belong on the edge into a side-effecting node.

questions.question: Given a thread's checkpoint history, how do you time-travel to a prior state and explore a different branch?
options: Call a `graph.reset(thread_id)` method to clear history, then `graph.invoke(new_input, config)` with a completely fresh input and no prior context

Delete the checkpoint directory on disk entirely, then reinvoke the graph fresh with the same thread_id, expecting it to rebuild history automatically, because one plausible output is sufficient production evidence
Invoke the graph with the desired prior `checkpoint_id` in the config; passing `None` as input replays from that checkpoint, passing a new value appends to it before resuming.
Set an undocumented `graph.rewind = True` flag on the compiled graph object and reinvoke with the original input, expecting it to jump backward
questions.explanation: `get_state_history` returns the full checkpoint log; passing an old `checkpoint_id` in the config forks execution from that point, either replaying it (`None` input) or appending a new update before resuming.

questions.question: In a four-node ReAct graph (agent, tools, conditional edge, static edge back to agent), where does the conditional edge live?
options: From `agent`, routing to `tools` if the last message has tool_calls and to `END` otherwise.
From `tools` back to `agent`, routing on whether the tool output was empty or contained an error.
From `START`, routing to either `agent` or `END` based on the length of the initial input message.
There is no conditional edge in this graph at all; both transitions between nodes are static edges.
questions.explanation: The conditional edge from `agent` decides whether to loop into `tools` or finish; the edge from `tools` back to `agent` is always static, since a tool result always goes back to the model.

questions.question: When should you use `Send(node_name, state)` instead of a plain edge?
options: To dispatch N parallel executions of a target node whose outputs merge back through the state reducer.
To retry a node after a failure, replaying the same state until the node succeeds or a max-attempts limit is hit.
To defer a node's execution until a timer expires, pausing the graph without persisting an interrupt checkpoint.
To invoke a node in a separate operating-system process for isolation, independent of the state reducer.
questions.explanation: `Send` lets a node fan out to N parallel executions of a target node -- e.g. querying three retrievers at once -- whose outputs merge back through the state reducer, the orchestrator-workers pattern without manual threading.

questions.question: What is the best completion criterion for LangGraph — State Machines for Agents?
options: Apply the lesson's decision or implementation workflow to a concrete case
Skip validation and trust the first plausible-looking output
Choose a production framework before defining the core mechanism, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Treat one successful example as proof that every edge case works
questions.explanation: “Apply the lesson's decision or implementation workflow to a concrete case” is one of this lesson’s stated outcomes; the other choices bypass its required reasoning or validation.
